title: Managing Environmental Impacts of Resource Use
seo_title: Year 12 Earth and Environmental Science: Managing Environmental Impacts Worksheets
standard_code: Earth and Environmental Science Unit 3: Living on Earth – managing Earth resources
standard_text: Environmental impacts of extracting and using resources (land clearing, acid mine drainage, tailings, emissions); environmental impact assessment; rehabilitation; ecological footprints; ecosystem services; the precautionary principle; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander land management. (Senior Secondary Earth and Environmental Science, Unit 3: Living on Earth – extracting, using and managing Earth resources)
meta_desc: Free Year 12 Earth and Environmental Science worksheets on environmental impacts: acid mine drainage, tailings, rehabilitation, EIA, ecological footprints, fisheries, offsets and cultural burning. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: EIA before approval; rehabilitation after closure.
body_html:
How to think about it

Extracting and using resources can clear habitat, pollute water (acid mine drainage, tailings), release greenhouse gases and change landscapes. An environmental impact assessment predicts these effects before a project is approved and sets conditions to reduce them.

Management includes rehabilitation (as at the Ranger uranium mine in Kakadu), recycling, quotas, offsets, the precautionary principle and the knowledge of Traditional Owners, such as cultural burning. Ecological footprints measure how much land and water a population needs.

Example

Footprint 6.8 global ha per person; Earth can supply 1.6. How many Earths?

6.8 ÷ 1.6

Answer: about 4.3 Earths

Example

Recycled aluminium uses 5% of the energy. Energy saved?

100% − 5%

Answer: 95%

Common mistakes

  • Thinking rehabilitation restores exactly the original ecosystem.
  • Saying ecosystem services are free and unlimited.
  • Forgetting that impacts can continue long after a mine closes.

faq.q: What makes acid mine drainage so hard to stop?
faq.a: Once sulfide minerals in waste rock are exposed to air and water they keep forming acid, sometimes for centuries, so waste must be covered or treated.

faq.q: Why is Indigenous land management important?
faq.a: Traditional Owners have managed country for tens of thousands of years; practices such as cultural burning reduce fuel loads and protect biodiversity.

items.q: William's class studies this problem: “Cars and factories burn fossil fuels.” Which solution would best reduce the impact?
c: keeping protected green spaces and wildlife corridors
public transit, electric vehicles and cleaner power
rain gardens and permeable footpath that soak up runoff
reusable bags and bans on single-use plastic
items.e: A good solution targets the cause of the impact.

items.q: What is cultural burning?
c: cool, low-intensity burns lit by Traditional Owners to manage country and reduce fuel loads
very hot fires lit in summer
items.e: It creates a mosaic of burnt and unburnt land.

items.q: What is mine rehabilitation?
c: returning a mined area to a safe, stable landscape, often with native vegetation
items.e: Ranger uranium mine in Kakadu is being rehabilitated.

items.q: What are 'ecosystem services'?
c: benefits people get from ecosystems, such as clean water, pollination and flood control
items.e: They are often hard to value in money.

items.q: How do fisheries quotas help keep fish stocks sustainable?
c: they limit the catch to below the rate at which the stock can replace itself
they increase the number of boats
items.e: Overfishing can make a stock collapse.

items.q: Kai's class studies this problem: “Forests are cleared for new houses.” Which solution would best reduce the impact?

planting grass buffer strips along the river and using less fertiliser
items.e: A good solution targets the cause of the impact.

items.q: Tom observes: “Forests are cleared for new houses.” What impact can this have?

items.e: Human activities can change Earth's systems.

items.q: What is a biodiversity offset?
c: protecting or restoring habitat elsewhere to make up for habitat lost to a development
items.e: Offsets are controversial because habitats are not identical.
